description: Our team consists of members of Georgia’s national AI Olympiad team. We have extensive experience competing in national and international hackathons and have worked on numerous projects involving ML, including some experience with astronomical data.
summary:
We help NASA find places on Earth that are similar to the Moon and Mars, so astronauts and equipment can be tested before going to space.

Using NASA data, we compare locations based on temperature, sunlight, slopes, and terrain. We also use an AI vision model called DINOv2 to compare how landscapes look.

We analyzed 35,107 locations across 35 million km² of Earth. One of our top matches for NASA’s planned Moon Base included Sedan Crater in Nevada, where Apollo astronauts trained in 1965.

But our main goal is to find new testing locations. Beyond 192 already known sites, we found a plateau in Argentina with slopes that closely match the Moon Base area (93/100 on our scale), and valleys in Algeria that resemble Warrego Valles on Mars.
details:
WHAT IS PROVING GROUND?

Everything built for the Moon or Mars is tested on Earth first, and a test is only as good as the ground it runs on.

Proving Ground grades places on Earth against one chosen Moon Base or Mars site, so rover teams and mission planners can train on ground matched to their destination and understand what that ground cannot test.

THE GAP

At the first Moon Base site, the Sun stays below about 2 degrees for 114 consecutive days (according to our model). NASA rehearses moonwalks in Arizona at night, using a lamp to simulate the Sun. The US Geological Survey lists 192 Earth analog sites as names and coordinates, and its 2024 report with NASA says a shared standard for evaluating analog sites is needed. We found no tool that grades an Earth location against one specific extraterrestrial target.

WHAT YOU DO IN THE APP
  1. Choose a target: one of 3 Moon Base sites or 23 Mars sites, and a test (driving a rover, landing, or working in low sunlight).
  2. Every Earth location receives a score out of 100 for each measure, and the app identifies which measures it fails.
  3. Compare any two locations using 3D terrain models built from real elevation data, displayed at the same scale.
  4. For the Moon's low sunlight, see the dates and minutes when a location experiences those conditions.
ONE EXAMPLE

Black Point lava flow in Arizona is where NASA tests rovers. Against Moon Base III, a flat plain, it scores 66 out of 100: recommended. Against Moon Base I, a steep polar ridge, the same location scores 30. Its slopes are too gentle, its lighting almost never matches, and it is never cold enough. A test site must be chosen for a specific target.

WHAT IT FOUND
  • An Apollo training ground, without being told. We searched all bare land on Earth outside Antarctica: 35,107 patches covering 35 million km². One of the six highest-ranked patches for Moon Base I contains Sedan Crater and Yucca Flat in Nevada, where Apollo crews trained starting in 1965. These locations were not included in our inputs; according to our random-patch test, this happens in about one out of every hundred draws.
  • A new place for the Moon, outside the 192 known sites. A 4,400 m plateau in Argentina's Puna de Jujuy, with a road 2 km away. Its slopes match the Moon Base I ridge with a score of 93/100; Black Point scores 30/100. This is a terrain match only: its lighting and temperature do not match, and it has not yet been tested on the ground.
  • A new place for Mars. A valley network in Algeria, the Chebka of the M'zab, resembles Warrego Valles. The system also ranks highly known geological analog pairs already used by scientists, including Iran's Lut Desert for Medusae Fossae (98/100).
  • Close to home. Didi Abuli in Georgia's Javakheti region matches the steepness of the Moon Base I ridge with a score of 88/100 (steepness only).
DOES IT WORK? BLIND TESTS
  • 9 Apollo training grounds, hidden from the search, rank above 80 out of 100 bare places. A random location scores 50.
  • 17 known Mars test sites, hidden from the program, rank above 73/100. Steepness alone scores 41.
  • Our sunlight model agrees with NASA's lunar illumination map at 92.5% of points.
HOW IT WORKS
  • NASA data: LOLA elevation (Moon, 20 m), MOLA (Mars), Diviner and MODIS temperatures, and MODIS land cover. Earth elevation comes from Copernicus GLO-30 and NOAA ETOPO 2022.
  • Machine learning, two jobs: DINOv2, a published vision transformer used with its original weights unchanged, converts ground images into 1,536 numerical features, allowing visually similar places to receive similar representations. We selected this method from 33 candidates using a development split and evaluated it once on a locked test set. Gradient-boosted decision trees learn from previously measured locations to select which places to measure next: four rounds, covering 1,052 locations measured at 30 m.
  • Separate environmental scores: Slopes, Sun height, temperature range, and bare ground are scored independently, so a high score on one measure cannot hide a failure on another.
WHO IT IS FOR, AND NEXT

University rover teams (134 entered the 2027 University Rover Challenge), analog mission organisers, and rover and lander developers.

Next steps: a first field check of a location identified by the program, finer terrain data for Mars, and additional measures such as minerals and radar roughness.

dataRefs: NASA Worldview / GIBS: the MODIS IGBP land-cover layer (MCD12Q1 v061, 2023), used as the bare-land mask that decides which 33,035 Earth tiles are searched.

NASA JPL Horizons (DE441), the Sun's position for the Moon's low-Sun numbers and a check of our Earth Sun positions (within 0.02 degrees); NASA POWER (rain, albedo, aerosol, snow cover; MERRA-2 and CERES based); Mars Global Surveyor TES albedo, emissivity, thermal inertia and dust cover, Mars Odyssey neutron hydrogen, and KRC modelled temperatures, read through ASU's JMARS; the MOLA-HRSC blended 200 m Mars DEM (NASA MOLA with ESA Mars Express HRSC, mosaic by USGS); SLDEM2015 (LOLA with JAXA Kaguya, mosaic by USGS).

NASA LRO LROC Narrow Angle and Wide Angle Camera images (Moon pictures and the 3D Moon blocks); NASADEM (a second elevation model to check the terrain match); NASA MODIS land surface temperature and land cover for all 35,107 searched Earth patches; NASA POWER snow cover for snow-free time; NASA Blue Marble (the world map); MRO Context Camera mosaic (Mars pictures; NASA/JPL/MSSS, The Murray Lab). The Sun positions for the South Pole result were checked against NASA JPL Horizons. NASA SP-2015-626 (Phinney 2015, "Science Training History of the Apollo Astronauts") is the source of the Apollo training grounds used in the blind test.
projectRefs: ESA / European Union, Copernicus DEM GLO-30 and GLO-90 (a Copernicus Data Space product; read from the AWS open-data copy): Earth terrain at 30 to 240 m for the 3D twins and the Moon Base terrain comparison. ESA Climate Change Initiative, Permafrost_cci v5.0 (2023 extent): Earth ice proxy.
ESA Mars Express HRSC (DLR), inside the MOLA-HRSC blended DEM; JAXA SELENE/Kaguya, inside SLDEM2015.
Mars Climate Database v6.2 (LMD, with CNES and ESA): Mars night temperature, day-night swing and dust (modelled).

NOAA NCEI, ETOPO 2022 Global Relief Model, doi:10.25921/fd45-gt74: Earth terrain tiles at about 925 m. Link: https://doi.org/10.25921/fd45-gt74 - European Commission JRC / Google, Global Surface Water v1.4 (Pekel et al. 2016, Nature 540, 418-422): lake flag.
DINOv2 ViT-B/14, Meta AI, Apache 2.0 (Oquab et al. 2023, arXiv:2304.07193), weights from timm on Hugging Face.
